To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ISIS-led attacks on Beirut, Paris, Baghdad were reported in different ways in the major news media outlets, that these differences were rooted in the Western construction, and the politics of suffering, and that this has important consequences for the training of health workers.
the media’s framing of the Paris, Beirut, Baghdad bombings in November 2014, and the subsequent medical humanitarian response, were influenced by the training of health care workers in the West.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the politics of representation, and the role that health professionals can and should play in challenging the dominant narratives of suffering and violence in the Middle East.
the ways in which language skews narratives of suffering and violence in the Middle East.
how media coverage can be used to promote social justice in the face of global violence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the media’s coverage of these events is a result of the way in which Western media and Western audiences perceive violence and suffering in different regions of the world, and that this perception is shaped by a variety of factors, including the media’s own agenda and the audience’s own expectations and interests.

the media coverage of the Paris attacks, and the subsequent lack of coverage of the Beirut and Baghdad bombings, is indicative of the ways in which the West constructs suffering and the emotivity of global violence.

the Western media’s selective and biased coverage of the attacks in Beirut and Baghdad, and its subsequent forgetting of these events, has contributed to a lack of understanding of the effects of violence and terrorism on the Middle Eastern population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Beirut bombings were a reminder of the ongoing and complex nature of the Syrian conflict and the need to understand the political and social factors that underlie the suffering of people in the region.
the Beirut bombings are an important example of the way in which Western media coverage of violence in the Middle East is skewed.

critical medical humanitarianism is the application of a medical lens to the study of the politics of humanitarianism, which is an approach that can help us understand how the politics of humanitarian action are shaped by the politics of the medical gaze.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the way that we frame suffering in the Middle Eastern context, both in media coverage and in the training of health practitioners, has consequences for the way that we respond to the needs of those suffering.

, in the context of global terrorism and war, the medical profession has a responsibility to critically engage with the ways in which the suffering of others is represented in the media and to promote more equitable, ethical, and just responses to global violence.
health professional training must address how the media shapes our understanding of violence and suffering, and the ways in which this shapes our understanding of the world.
